items.q: Service lifecycle: what are the two kinds of services? What are the real traps?
shortAnswer: A started service runs until `stopSelf()` or `stopService()`. A bound service lives while at least one `ServiceConnection` is connected.
`onStartCommand` returns `START_STICKY`, `START_NOT_STICKY`, or `START_REDELIVER_INTENT`, which decides what the system does if it kills your process.
The classic trap: a Service does not run on its own thread — callbacks land on the main thread; forgetting `stopSelf` leaks it.
items.answer:
#### Two flavors, two lifetimes
A **started service** is launched with `startService()` (or `startForegroundService()`) and keeps running until it calls `stopSelf()` or an outside caller calls `stopService()`. A **bound service** is created with `bindService()` and is destroyed when the last `ServiceConnection` disconnects (`onUnbind` then `onDestroy`). A service can be both at once.

#### The callbacks
`onCreate` runs once, then `onStartCommand(intent, flags, startId)` runs per start, `onBind` serves binding, `onDestroy` is final cleanup. Every callback runs on the **main thread**, so real work needs a coroutine, a thread, or WorkManager.

#### The return values
`START_STICKY` restarts the service with a null intent after a kill; `START_NOT_STICKY` does not restart; `START_REDELIVER_INTENT` restarts with the same intent. Pick based on whether the work must survive a process kill.

#### The traps
- A started service that never calls `stopSelf(startId)` leaks until the system kills the process — a `start` without a matching stop is the standard bug.
- `startForegroundService()` without a `startForeground()` call inside ~10 seconds throws `ForegroundServiceDidNotStartInTimeException`.
- Saying "services run in the background" is the classic wrong answer — they run on your process's main thread.

code.caption: Started service with safe stop and off-main work

followUps: What does `START_STICKY` do to your `intent` when the system restarts you?
When would you use a bound service instead of a started one?
Why is a Service not a background thread?
traps: Saying a Service runs on its own thread. All service callbacks run on the main thread by default.
Forgetting `stopSelf` — the service keeps running (and its process stays alive) long after the user is done.

items.q: ContentProvider lifecycle: how does it work, why does it matter?
shortAnswer: A provider starts before `Application.onCreate`: the system calls `Application.attachBaseContext`, then every declared provider's `onCreate`, and only then your `Application.onCreate`.
That ordering is why libraries use a dummy provider to auto-initialize: their code runs ahead of your app, and you cannot reorder it.
Provider methods (`query`, `insert`, `update`, `delete`) run on the calling binder thread, not the main thread — a common wrong assumption.
items.answer:
#### When it starts
The system instantiates every manifest-declared `ContentProvider` in the process's start sequence: `Application.attachBaseContext()` runs, then each provider's `onCreate()`, then `Application.onCreate()`. So a provider's `onCreate` runs *before* your app's own initialization. That is why `androidx.startup` exists — libraries register a single `Initializer` provider and you declare dependencies and ordering instead of guessing.

#### The trap that causes crashes
A library that self-installs via a provider does its work before `Application.onCreate`. You cannot set up logging or a crash handler and expect it to catch that provider's failures, and you cannot easily defer it (though `androidx.startup` lets you disable individual initializers). The `onCreate` of a provider runs on the main thread, so anything slow there delays every cold start.

#### The callbacks
`query`, `insert`, `update`, `delete`, `getType`, `openFile`, `applyBatch` are the data API. They execute on the **binder thread** that delivered the call — not the main thread — so a slow query blocks the caller's thread, not your main thread, but your provider must still be thread-safe.

#### Versioning
`onCreate` and the data methods never restart for a configuration change; the provider lives for the process. Version and notify: `getContext().getContentResolver().notifyChange(...)` and `getType` matter for correct `ContentObserver` behaviour.

code.caption: A provider whose onCreate is cheap and whose methods are thread-safe

followUps: Why do libraries register an initializer as a ContentProvider instead of using `Application.onCreate`?
Which thread do `query`/`insert` run on, and what does that imply for your DB access?
How does `androidx.startup` change the ordering story?
traps: Saying provider methods run on the main thread. They run on the binder thread that called in.
Doing heavy work in the provider's `onCreate` and not realizing it runs before `Application.onCreate`, inflating cold start.

items.q: How does a BroadcastReceiver work? Where do people misuse it?
shortAnswer: `onReceive` runs on the main thread and only lives for that call. Too long — ~10 s foreground, 60 s background — the system flags it.
Manifest-registered receivers can receive implicit broadcasts but must declare `android:exported`. Since Android 8, most implicit broadcasts are banned for manifest receivers anyway.
The classic misuse is starting an `Activity` or doing real work in `onReceive` — that is an ANR, a trampoline violation, and often both.
items.answer:
#### The contract
A `BroadcastReceiver` has one meaningful callback: `onReceive(context, intent)`. It runs on the **main thread**, and the receiver instance is only guaranteed alive for the duration of that call. Do heavy work past it and the system assumes you hung: ~10 s (foreground) or ~60 s (background) is the ANR window.

#### Two registration types
- **Manifest-registered** — declared in the manifest, delivered even when the app is dead, must set `android:exported`. Since Android 8.0 most implicit broadcasts (system-wide intents without an explicit package) are no longer delivered to manifest receivers, so this type is mostly for `BOOT_COMPLETED`, custom explicit broadcasts, and alarms.
- **Context-registered** (`registerReceiver` in `onStart`, unregister in `onStop`) — only live while registered, gets all broadcasts including explicit ones, and you choose `RECEIVER_EXPORTED`/`RECEIVER_NOT_EXPORTED` on Android 14+.

#### goAsync
For work that must outlive `onReceive`, call `goAsync()` to get a `PendingResult`, run off-main, and finish with `pendingResult.finish()`. The window still applies — finish within the timeout or the system kills you.

#### The classic misuses
- Starting an Activity from `onReceive` — blocked for trampolines since Android 12, and background-activity-start limits apply.
- Blocking inside `onReceive` on a network call — main thread, so an ANR.
- Registering a receiver but never unregistering — a leak.

code.caption: goAsync for work that outlives onReceive

followUps: What changed for manifest receivers on Android 8.0?
When is `goAsync` the right answer and when is WorkManager better?
What does `RECEIVER_EXPORTED` vs `RECEIVER_NOT_EXPORTED` mean for security?
traps: Thinking a receiver 'runs in the background'. `onReceive` is main-thread and short-lived.
Starting an Activity from a receiver — blocked as a notification trampoline and by background-activity-start rules.

items.q: What is the difference between the Fragment lifecycle and the Fragment view lifecycle? Why does it keep causing bugs?
shortAnswer: On the back stack the Fragment survives but its View is destroyed; the View's own lifecycle ends at `onDestroyView`.
Observing with `this` instead of `viewLifecycleOwner` binds the observer to the Fragment — it outlives the destroyed view and re-registers on return.
The fix: do everything view-related against `viewLifecycleOwner`, and null out `ViewBinding` in `onDestroyView`.
items.answer:
#### Two lifecycles, deliberately out of sync
When a Fragment is popped onto the back stack, the transaction **destroys its View** but keeps the Fragment instance. The instance lifecycle (`onAttach` → `onCreate` → `onDestroy` → `onDetach`) and the view lifecycle (`onCreateView` → `onViewCreated` → `onDestroyView`) diverge. Navigating away destroys the view; the Fragment, its ViewModel, and its saved state survive. Navigating back recreates the view.

#### The bug this causes
Observing a `LiveData`/`Flow` with `this` as the owner binds the observer to the Fragment, not the view. The observer stays subscribed after `onDestroyView`, and when the Fragment returns you re-subscribe — two live observers, one rendering into the now-recreated view, plus a leaked reference to the old view. That is the classic "I see double updates" or "my screen updates from the back stack" bug.

#### The rules
- Use `viewLifecycleOwner` for anything touching the view: observers, `lifecycleScope`, `repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED)`, listeners.
- Null out `ViewBinding` in `onDestroyView` so you don't keep a destroyed hierarchy alive.
- Keep Fragment-scoped things (the ViewModel is fine to fetch with `by viewModels()`) on the Fragment; they legitimately outlive the view.
- `viewLifecycleOwner` is only available after `onCreateView` — code running before that must not touch it.

code.caption: view-scoped observation vs the leaking alternative

followUps: What exactly happens to the ViewModel when the view is destroyed but the Fragment lives?
Why can't you touch `viewLifecycleOwner` inside `onCreate`?
How does this interact with `FragmentResultListener` scoping?
traps: Saying the Fragment's view dies with the Fragment. On the back stack they diverge.
Using `this` as the lifecycle owner for view work — duplicate observers and a leaked view hierarchy.

items.q: What happens on a configuration change? What actually survives it?
shortAnswer: A configuration change destroys and recreates the `Activity`, but the process stays alive — anything in memory can survive if the framework keeps it.
`ViewModel` survives because it lives in a `ViewModelStore` the framework retains. Statics, singletons, and `Application` also survive — process-scoped.
Put view state you care about in `SavedStateHandle` or `rememberSaveable`. The trick is to persist identifiers, not payloads.
items.answer:
#### What happens
A config change (rotation, dark mode, locale, window resize, keyboard) makes the system destroy the Activity and recreate it. The **process is untouched** — so anything process-scoped survives: static fields, singletons, `Application`, thread pools, disk cache. The Activity itself is rebuilt from scratch and `onSaveInstanceState`'s `Bundle` is handed to the new instance.

#### What survives and how
- **`ViewModel`**: survives, because the framework retains its `ViewModelStore` in a `NonConfigurationInstance` between the old and new Activity. That is why repositories and `MutableStateFlow` in a ViewModel survive rotation.
- **`SavedStateHandle`**: part of the ViewModel, backed by the saved-instance-state `Bundle`, so it survives config change *and* process death.
- **`rememberSaveable` / `onSaveInstanceState`**: Compose/View UI state, keyed into the same Bundle.
- **Nothing else on the Activity side**: views, listeners, `Dialog`s, and Fragment *views* are rebuilt.

#### The traps
- `android:configChanges` on the manifest suppresses the recreate and lets you handle it yourself — but you must then re-read resources, re-apply dark mode, and resize manually. It is almost always the wrong answer.
- A config change is **not** process death. Saying "the system saves and restores everything" is wrong on both counts — statics survive the first and not the second.
- Locale, `uiMode`, `fontScale`, `screenSize`, and `density` all trigger recreation; apps that only handle rotation get burned by `uiMode` when the user flips dark mode.

code.caption: What survives rotation — the ViewModel path

followUps: Why is `android:configChanges` usually a bad idea?
What survives a config change that does NOT survive process death?
Which configuration changes trigger recreation beyond rotation?
traps: Confusing configuration change with process death — the survival rules are opposite for statics and ViewModels.
Handling only rotation. `uiMode`, `locale`, `fontScale`, and `screenSize` all recreate the Activity too.

items.q: Predictive back is on by default at current targetSdk levels. How does `OnBackPressedDispatcher` work? What changes with the new gesture?
shortAnswer: `OnBackPressedDispatcher` runs callbacks last-registered-first, so the newest `OnBackPressedCallback` wins — `addCallback` on entry, `remove` on exit.
Predictive back turns the instant pop into a swipe animation: the system asks *in advance* whether a callback will handle the gesture — register callbacks early.
The traps are the opposite of old `onBackPressed`: never react *after* the event — a callback enabled at the wrong time breaks the back-to-home animation.
items.answer:
#### The dispatcher
`OnBackPressedDispatcher` is the single point that receives the back event and fans it out. Callbacks are invoked in reverse registration order (LIFO): register the most specific one last so it wins. `addCallback(lifecycleOwner, enabled) { ... }` ties it to a lifecycle — the callback is dropped automatically when the owner leaves `STARTED`. You must `remove()` a callback when the screen exits or it stays and eats back presses.

#### Predictive back changes the model
The old model was **post-hoc**: the system finishes, you handle the aftermath. Predictive back is **ahead-of-time**: the system must know before the gesture completes whether you will intercept, so it can run the exit animation as the user swipes. That means:
- Set `android:enableOnBackInvokedCallback="true"` (default for apps targeting 36 on current releases; explicit earlier).
- Register callbacks before the user can gesture, and keep them enabled exactly while the condition holds — toggling `enabled` is the signal.
- For animated control use `PredictiveBackHandler`/`OnBackAnimationCallback` receiving a `BackEventCompat` with `progress` and `swipeEdge`.

#### What breaks
A callback registered after the gesture started, or one that logs/acts after the event, silently breaks the animation or the pop. Intercepting back at the root Activity kills the back-to-home animation entirely.

code.caption: LIFO callbacks: dialog wins over navigation while open

followUps: What does `addCallback(lifecycleOwner, ...)` buy you compared to a raw callback?
Why must predictive-back callbacks be registered before the gesture starts?
How does `PRIORITY_SYSTEM_NAVIGATION_OBSERVER` differ from intercepting callbacks?
traps: Handling back in `onBackPressed`/after-the-fact — that model is deprecated and breaks the predictive animation.
Forgetting `remove()` on a callback, so a stale screen eats every subsequent back press.

items.q: Startup sequence from the launcher tap to the first frame — where do the costs live?
shortAnswer: The launcher asks the system to start your app; a dead process is forked by `zygote` with your package's uid.
Inside the fork: `Application.attachBaseContext` → every manifest `ContentProvider.onCreate` → `Application.onCreate` → then the first `Activity` is created, measured, laid out, and drawn.
Every stage is a tax on cold start. Providers and `Application.onCreate` run before the first frame — move any work out of them.
items.answer:
#### The fork
`zygote` is the template process: it preloads the ART runtime and framework classes so every app process is a fork of it. For a cold start, the system `ActivityManager` asks zygote to fork a process with your app's uid and main entry — the fork is why class loading is already warm even though your code is not. Then the process runs its `ActivityThread.main`, which instantiates `Application`.

#### The ordering that matters
`Application.attachBaseContext` runs first (before any `onCreate` — this is where your `Context` is set up). Then every manifest-declared `ContentProvider` is instantiated and its `onCreate` called — this is before `Application.onCreate`, and it is why `androidx.startup` exists. Only then does `Application.onCreate` run, followed by the launch `Activity`: `onCreate`/`onStart`/`onResume`, layout inflation or composition, and finally the first drawn frame.

#### Where the cost hides
- Anything synchronous in `Application.onCreate` or a provider's `onCreate` delays the first frame directly.
- Class verification and loading: interpreted then JIT-compiled on first use — the cold-start tax baseline profiles exist to remove.
- The first frame also waits for the display: `Choreographer` draws when the next vsync arrives, so a heavy first composition pushes the frame past it and the launcher holds your splash screen visibly longer.

#### The lever
Move work out of the pre-frame path: defer library init (App Startup), avoid disk and network before the first frame, and ship baseline profiles so the startup path is AOT-compiled.

code.caption: Deferring non-critical init past the first frame

followUps: Why does forking from zygote make class loading cheap but still leave your code cold?
Where do ContentProvider-based initializers sit in the sequence, and what do you do about them?
What is the relationship between cold start and the first `Choreographer` frame?
traps: Placing library initialization in `Application.onCreate` and not noticing it runs before the first frame.
Treating a splash screen as a startup fix — it makes startup *feel* faster, it does not make it faster.

items.q: What does `android:exported` control? How do you keep your components safe?
shortAnswer: `android:exported` decides whether other apps can start or bind your component — mandatory when a component has an intent filter and you target Android 12+.
A filtered component without `exported` fails the build. A component without a filter defaults to `false`, which is the safe direction.
An exported component is a public attack surface: validate every incoming intent, and prefer `exported="false"` plus a `signature`-level permission.
items.answer:
#### The flag
`android:exported="true"` means other apps can start your Activity, bind your Service, or send to your Receiver; `false` means only your app (and the system) can. Since targeting Android 12 the attribute is **required whenever the component declares an intent filter** — a manifest with an exported-less filtered component fails at install/build with a clear error. Components without a filter default to `false`, which is the safe direction.

#### Why it matters
An exported Activity is a public entry point. Attackers can craft an intent that starts it with hostile extras — which is precisely why deep links and inter-app launches are security reviews' favourite target. An exported Service or Receiver can be driven to do work on demand, and an exported `ContentProvider` hands out your data by default. The `ContentProvider` default is `true` (to satisfy the platform's content URI machinery) unless you set it — the single most common accidental data exposure.

#### The rules that keep you safe
- `exported="false"` unless you can name the other app and the exact use case.
- If another app needs access, prefer `android:permission` with `protectionLevel="signature"` so only your signed apps can reach it.
- For a provider, `exported="true"` only where needed plus `android:grantUriPermissions` and per-URI permissions, not blanket exposure.
- Validate every extra and the calling package (`getCallingPackage`) inside exported components — the framework will not do it for you.
- `activity-alias` inherits the target's exported state; keep its own filter honest.

code.caption: A provider sealed to signature-signed callers only
code.src:
<!-- AndroidManifest.xml -->
<provider
    android:name=".NotesProvider"
    android:authorities="${applicationId}.notes"
    android:exported="true"
    android:permission="com.example.app.READ_NOTES"
    android:grantUriPermissions="false" />

<permission
    android:name="com.example.app.READ_NOTES"
    android:protectionLevel="signature" />

// Activity that receives an external intent must not trust its extras:
fun onCreate() {
    val itemId = intent.getStringExtra("itemId")
        ?.takeIf { it.matches(Regex("[a-zA-Z0-9_-]{1,32}")) }
    if (itemId != null) openItem(itemId) else finish()
}

followUps: Why does the `ContentProvider` default differ from other components?
What does a `signature` protection level protect against that a custom runtime permission does not?
How does `android:exported` interact with deep-link intent filters?
traps: Leaving a `ContentProvider` exported by default — it is the one component whose default is the unsafe value.
Treating `exported="true"` as harmless when the component has no intent filter; the surface is still there for explicit intents.

items.q: What is intent redirection? Why did Android 14 start blocking implicit intents to internal components?
shortAnswer: Intent redirection: an exported component receives an attacker's intent and forwards it on, carrying the original grants and flags with it.
Android 14 (targetSdk 34+) blocks implicit intents that resolve to your own non-exported components — so use explicit intents for internal navigation.
The fix: never forward a received intent. Build a fresh `Intent`, copy only validated data, and drop the caller's flags and URI grants.
items.answer:
#### The attack
An exported component is a funnel. An attacker sends an intent into it; the component does `startActivity(intent)` (or passes it to a `PendingIntent` or `getActivity`) — and the forwarded intent still carries the attacker's action, data URI, component target, and **grant flags**. The grant is the payoff: the attacker gets read access to a URI the victim app would never have granted, or a privileged action launched in a privileged context.

#### What Android 14 changed
For apps targeting 34+, an **implicit intent** (no explicit component) that resolves to one of your own **non-exported** components throws — the system refuses to let a broadly-typed intent reach an internal component. That kills the old "implicit self-broadcast" pattern and forces explicit `Intent(this, Target::class.java)` for internal work.

#### The hardening checklist
- Never re-launch a received `Intent`. Copy what you need into a **new** `Intent` and validate every field.
- Strip flags: `intent.flags = 0` (or keep only ones you set), and remove `FLAG_GRANT_READ_URI_PERMISSION`/`FLAG_GRANT_WRITE_URI_PERMISSION` unless you're intentionally handing a grant.
- Apply `StrictMode.VmPolicy.Builder().detectUnsafeIntentLaunch()` to find forwards at development time.
- For `PendingIntent`, prefer `FLAG_IMMUTABLE` so the recipient cannot fill in extras.
- Treat the component that received the intent as untrusted input — same discipline as a deep link.

code.caption: Forwarding safely: new intent, validated data, no grants

followUps: How do URI permission grants survive an intent forward?
What breaks when you send an implicit intent to your own non-exported receiver on Android 14?
Why does `detectUnsafeIntentLaunch` only help in debug?
traps: Forwarding the received intent unchanged, thinking the framework re-validates it. Grants and flags travel with it.
Using implicit intents for internal navigation — blocked for non-exported targets since Android 14.

items.q: How do multi-window, resizability, and the display cutout change what your Activity code must handle?
shortAnswer: In multi-window, an `Activity` can be visible but not focused, and it can resize while running — so `onPause` no longer means hidden.
A display cutout removes part of the screen: `WindowInsets.displayCutout` reports where, and `layoutInDisplayCutoutMode` decides whether you draw behind it.
Foldables and large screens are the same problem: a configuration change with a new window size and maybe a hinge.
items.answer:
#### Multi-window changes the lifecycle story
Since split-screen, an Activity can be **visible but not focused** (a paused activity on screen) and its size can change while running. Two consequences: stop treating `onPause` as "hidden" — use `onStop` — and handle window resizes gracefully (`onConfigurationChanged` with a new `screenWidthDp`, or Compose's adaptive layout). An app that only ever handled rotation is broken in split-screen.

#### Resizability
`android:resizeableActivity="true"` (default) opts into resizing. Large-screen expectations keep rising: current releases push apps to support resizing and to stop locking orientation. When the window resizes, the system either recreates the Activity (a config change — your ViewModel survives) or delivers `onConfigurationChanged` if you suppressed recreation.

#### Display cutouts
A cutout (notch/punch-hole) consumes inset space at an edge. Read `WindowInsets.displayCutout` to get the cutout rect, and set `layoutInDisplayCutoutMode` (`default`, `shortEdges`, `never`) per-window. Drawing a status bar over the cutout is fine; placing your content behind it without insets is not.

#### Foldables
A foldable is a large screen that can change size — the hinge is a display feature reported through `WindowLayoutInfo`/`WindowInfoTracker`, and opening/closing it is a window size change plus a config change. Same rules: observe window metrics, handle the size change, never hard-code a phone-sized layout.

code.caption: Reacting to window metrics instead of assuming phone-sized

followUps: Why is `onPause` not a reliable 'hidden' signal anymore?
What breaks when you lock orientation on a foldable or tablet at current targetSdk?
How do cutout insets differ from system-bar insets?
traps: Building for one window size and letting the rest break — split-screen, foldable-open, and large screens all exercise the code paths you skipped.
Drawing behind a cutout without reading the inset, so content sits under the punch-hole.
